title: "AI Policy" Considerations for Schools
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard sets out what schools should weigh when writing a generative AI policy, arguing that the policy is unworkable without basic AI literacy for staff and students. He starts from assumptions he treats as facts: students want to use the tools, schools cannot realistically stop them, technology is changing faster than policy cycles, and the gap between schools is growing. He then moves through practical advice (keep it to one page, avoid the blanket term AI, update only when essential), legal issues (privacy, plagiarism detector false positives, age limits, human-in-the-loop, discrimination, hallucination), and guidance for teachers and administrators. His ethical move is to shift attention from policing cheating toward the school's obligation to prepare students for an AI world. He closes with staged action items for immediate, three-month, six-month and nine-month horizons.
points: A policy cannot be implemented without AI literacy, because teachers and students who do not understand the tools cannot interpret or enforce rules about them.
Bauschard argues schools cannot control student use, so policy should aim to influence it and secure buy-in from the whole community.
Detector scores should only start a conversation with a student, never ground discipline, given false positives and the lack of anything to verify suspected output against.
Practical drafting advice includes keeping the policy to one page, avoiding the word AI in bans, and distinguishing supported use from merely allowed use.
He reframes the ethical question from stopping cheating to the school's duty to prepare students, noting a widening gap between schools that teach with AI and those that ban it.
quotes: Schools cannot control the use of generative AI by students, but they can influence it. Unless your school has a no devices policy

Schools can try to play whack-a-mole and restrain all of those places, but the minute students step off a school wireless network or device (including when in school), they have access to all of these sites.

Students want to learn to work with GAI. Schools are apprehensive about GAI for a variety of reasons, but students want to work with it because they know they will use it in the workforce. For this reason, they don’t necessarily consider it to be cheating; in fact, they see that by being denied it, they are being cheated out of learning to prepare for the workforce.

Don’t say “AI,” especially if you’re banning it. “AI” is used in many tools, from Google search to Canva to Quizlet. Saying you are “banning AI” will instantly undermine the credibility of your policy and destroy your credibility with anyone who knows anything about the technology.

Simply opening the door on a school day creates liability. So does allowing kids to put on helmets and slam their heads into each other on school property. Schools take liability risks because they know those risks are important to academic gains and social development. If we can allow kids to smash their heads into each other in 90+ degree heat, we can allow them to use generative AI.

If your institution doesn’t have a policy yet, this may not be possible, but over time, you should reach out to your community. As discussed at the beginning, it is very difficult for schools to regulate this technology, so the only way to make it work is with buy-in.
I don’t think you can have an AI Policy without establishing some basic AI literacy amongst faculty and students; how can they otherwise understand it?
